How this book matches your exam. Research check: this book follows NCERT Class 11 Biology Chapter 1 (The Living World) and Chapter 2 (Biological Classification), for the CBSE 2026–27 session. These chapters sit in Unit I, Diversity of Living Organisms, which carries 15 of the 70 theory marks together with the Plant and Animal Kingdom chapters (Book 2). Expect definitions, comparisons, classification tables and diagram-based questions. The rationalised NCERT book has dropped the sections "What is Living?" and "Taxonomical Aids", so this book does not drill them.

Each unit ends with a 10-mark practice set. The marking points are our own, not the official CBSE marking scheme.

Unit 1 of 10: Diversity and the Science of Taxonomy

Key ideas

  • Biodiversity: the number and types of organisms on Earth; about 1.7–1.8 million species have been described, and many more remain undiscovered.
  • Identification: finding the correct name of an organism. Nomenclature: naming it by agreed rules. Classification: grouping organisms into convenient categories based on easily observable characters.
  • Taxonomy: characterisation, identification, nomenclature and classification. It now uses external and internal structure, cell structure, development and ecology.
  • Systematics (from systema, "systematic arrangement"): taxonomy plus evolutionary relationships between organisms.
  • Classification makes the study of a huge variety of organisms possible: we learn group features instead of every single organism.

Worked examples

Example 1: How is systematics broader than taxonomy? Answer: taxonomy identifies, names and classifies; systematics also considers evolutionary relationships among organisms.

10-mark practice set

  1. (1 mark, MCQ) The process of finding the correct name of an organism is called: (a) classification (b) identification (c) nomenclature (d) characterisation. Answer: (b).
  2. (1 mark) About how many species have been described so far? Answer: about 1.7–1.8 million.
  3. (2 marks) Name the four basic processes of taxonomy. Answer: characterisation and identification (1); nomenclature and classification (1).
  4. (3 marks) Why is classification necessary? Give three reasons. Answer: huge number of organisms can't be studied one by one (1); grouping by shared features makes study easier (1); shows relationships between groups (1).
  5. (3 marks) Distinguish between taxonomy and systematics, with the meaning of the word "systematics". Answer: taxonomy — identification, naming and classification (1); systematics — also includes evolutionary relationships (1); from Latin systema, systematic arrangement (1).

Common mistakes

  1. Identification = nomenclature. 2. Systematics = taxonomy. 3. Forgetting characterisation. 4. Exact species count claims. 5. Classification without basis.

Quick recall

  1. Biodiversity? 2. Identification? 3. Systematics adds? 4. Basis of classification? 5. Described species?

Answers: 1) Number and types of organisms. 2) Finding the correct name. 3) Evolutionary relationships. 4) Observable characters. 5) About 1.7–1.8 million.
